title: Public Sector Banks (PSBs) grow stronger with prudent banking practices and strong underwriting capabilities
subtitle:
PSB asset quality at all-time high with historically low stressed assets

PSBs’ gross advances reach ₹127 lakh crore with 18.8% y-o-y growth

Retail, agriculture and MSME advances grow at 17.0%, 19.5% and 20.4%, respectively

Total deposits grow to ₹165.2 lakh crore at 12.9% y-o-y

Net NPA ratio at 0.33%; Gross NPAs fall to ₹44,100 crore
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 NOV 2026 6:47PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Public Sector Banks (PSBs) continue to grow rapidly with high asset quality, ably supported by reform enabled prudent credit underwriting and effective risk management policies. The systemic reforms instituted in PSBs are showing fruitful results in the form of high quality rapidly paced credit growth across sectors, especially productive credit growth. Credit delivery to MSMEs and corporates by PSBs has also shown remarkable improvement with both growing at fast pace along with Agriculture and Retail. At the same time, the asset quality continues to improve to all-time best, supported by low slippages and strong recoveries in impaired assets. The institutionalisation of reforms has created a strong system of governance led banking in PSBs, supporting economic upcycle.
PSBs’ advances are growing rapidly at 15.1% in last 5-years and reached ₹127 lakh crore as on 30.9.2026. However, at the same time PSBs are also showing signs of strong prudence in credit underwriting through rapidly declining slippages. As against advances of ₹67.7 lakh crore as on 31.3.2021, the slippages were as high as ₹1.44 lakh crore at a rate of 2.35% in FY2021-22. It has now come down to just ₹38,780 crore against advances of ₹127 lakh crore in H1FY2026-27, recording slippage ratio of just 0.62%, a remarkable sign of growth with prudence.
The credit growth is not only prudent in terms of asset quality, but also is well diversified and focused across sectors. PSBs are extending credit to productive and consumptive sectors simultaneously with high credit growth in Retail, Agriculture, MSME and corporate sectors evenly balanced. While credit to retail and agriculture continues at strong rate over past more than 5-years, credit to MSME and corporates have also picked up to outpace other sectors marginally.
Looking at bank-wise performance in terms of credit growth, almost all banks are evenly extending credit with Bank of Maharashtra outpacing others, while large banks such as, State Bank of India, Canara Bank, Bank of Baroda and Punjab National Bank are also growing rapidly.
Even with high credit growth, continued improvement in slippages ratio is observed across banks with only Punjab & Sind Bank recording marginal decline in slippage ratio, though already having low slippage ratio of 0.57%. Amongst large banks, State Bank of India, Punjab National Bank and Canara Bank continues to have low slippages. All PSBs now have slippage ratio of less than 1%.
The lower slippages have helped banks in maintaining low NPA levels, though aided by sufficient provisioning and strong recovery also. As a result of combined efforts in prudent underwriting and efficient collections, PSBs are maintaining significantly low net NPAs of 0.33%, amounting Rs. 44,100 crore only, in advances of more than Rs. 127 lakh crore. PSBs continue to have significantly low stress in the form of SMAs also, with aggregate advances of only ₹18,800 crore falling in SMA 1 and 2 amongst advances above ₹5 crore. PSBs continue to improve in SMA levels also with ratio of SMA 1 & 2 advances of above ₹5 crore to total standard advances being only 0.14% as on 30.9.2026, as against 0.24% as on 30.9.2025.
Prudent credit underwriting and efficient risk management practices are paving way for a stronger and robust banking sector having capability to support credit needs of the economy for long term.

In a major crackdown on illegal wildlife trafficking, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), in a joint operation with Bihar State Police, has seized 19.39 kg elephant ivory and apprehended four persons involved in its illegal trade in West Champaran district of Bihar, near the Indo-Nepal border.
In an intelligence led operation, DRI officers, in coordination with Bihar State Police, intercepted four persons travelling on two two-whelers yesterday. One of the suspects was carrying a bag suspected to contain elephant ivory. The suspects attempted to flee and resisted the officers but were successfully apprehended. On examination, 19.39 kg elephant ivory was recovered and seized under the relevant provisions of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
Elephants are protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and are listed in Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). Trade in ivory is prohibited under Indian law, and illegal trafficking poses a serious threat to elephant conservation and biodiversity.
The operation underscores DRI’s commitment to combating wildlife trafficking and dismantling networks involved in the illegal trade of protected species through intelligence-led enforcement and close coordination with other law enforcement agencies.

Conference deliberates on strengthening food safety enforcement, drug quality oversight, laboratory infrastructure, digital traceability and consumer awareness
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:

content:
A National-Level Conference on Food Safety and Drug Administration was held today in Bengaluru, Karnataka, under the theme
“Safer Food, Safer Medicine, Healthier Nation”
, with a focus on strengthening food and drug regulatory systems through coordinated action, effective enforcement and enhanced institutional capacity.
The Conference brought together senior representatives of the Government of India, State and Union Territory Governments, regulatory authorities, public health institutions and enforcement agencies to deliberate on key challenges and identify measures to further strengthen food and drug safety across the country.
Addressing the Conference, Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava described food and drug regulatory authorities as the vanguards of public health, entrusted with the responsibility of safeguarding the health and well-being of every citizen. She emphasised that regulators must discharge their responsibilities effectively, efficiently and with integrity, while maintaining a balance between public health protection and ease of doing business.
Highlighting that regulatory decisions have a direct bearing on public health as well as on food business operators, manufacturers and retailers, she stressed the need to focus on essential regulatory requirements and strengthen coordination between Central and State authorities.
On food safety, the Union Health Secretary emphasised that regulatory efforts must go beyond preventing food adulteration and the sale of unsafe food to also promote healthy eating and better nutrition. She underlined the importance of capacity-building and the wider adoption of safe food-handling practices.
Referring to the perpetual validity of food safety licences, she noted that this places greater responsibility on regulatory authorities to ensure effective monitoring and robust, risk-based inspections. She also invited States to share their feedback on the risk-based inspection mechanism of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).
On drug regulation, Smt. Srivastava emphasised the need to strengthen State-level regulatory capacity through improved inspection mechanisms and greater adoption of technology. She highlighted the proposal for a sub-national assessment framework, aligned with World Health Organization (WHO) maturity-level parameters, to assess the capacity and performance of State drug regulatory systems.
She encouraged States to review SHRESHT (State Health Regulatory Excellence Index), the virtual assessment tool, and share their feedback to help strengthen the framework. Underscoring the importance of State participation in the conceptualisation of the Digital Drug Regulatory System (DDRS), she called upon States to contribute their practical experience and suggestions to inform its development.
She also stressed the need to strengthen transparency and accountability in clinical trials, including in the functioning of Contract Research Organisations (CROs).
Conference deliberates on strengthening regulatory frameworks, surveillance and enforcement
The Conference provided a platform for detailed deliberations on strengthening food and drug regulatory frameworks, improving surveillance and enforcement, augmenting institutional and laboratory capacities, and promoting coordinated action between Central and State authorities. The discussions reaffirmed that access to safe food and safe, effective and quality-assured medicines is fundamental to protecting public health, preventing avoidable illness and maintaining consumer confidence.
The food safety sessions reviewed the implementation of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with particular emphasis on risk-based inspections, surveillance, enforcement, food testing and evidence-based regulatory action. The discussions also covered good practices adopted by States in implementing food safety regulations, along with emerging challenges relating to e-commerce, novel foods and consumer trust.
The drug safety sessions focused on measures to combat spurious and adulterated medicines and address issues relating to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances through strengthened inter-State coordination in investigation and enforcement. Other key areas included greater uniformity in licensing and regulatory practices, risk-based inspections and surveillance, and adherence to good manufacturing and distribution practices under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and the Rules thereunder.
The deliberations also addressed emerging challenges in the pharmaceutical sector, strategies to sustain India's position as the “Pharmacy of the World”, and the role of next-generation cellular and molecular platforms in accelerating discovery and therapeutic applications.

title: Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava highlights Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s emphasis on greater investment and public-private partnerships in the health sector
subtitle:
Addresses National Level Orientation Workshop on National Health Mission and Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission in Bengaluru

PM-ABHIM has approved 19,983 infrastructure units across the country, including 2,151 Block Public Health Units, 744 Integrated Public Health Laboratories and 631 Critical Care Blocks

Emphasises strengthening public health infrastructure, disease surveillance and emergency preparedness through coordinated Centre-State efforts

Calls upon States and UTs to accelerate implementation of PM-ABHIM and ensure timely operationalisation of approved infrastructure
ministry: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 NOV 2026 4:28PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Health Secretary Smt. Punya Salila Srivastava addressed the National Level Orientation Workshop on the National Health Mission (NHM) and the Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) in Bengaluru, Karnataka. The two-day workshop, which commenced on 25 November 2026, brought together representatives from States and Union Territories and senior officials of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to review the progress of the two national missions, deliberate on implementation priorities and strengthen coordination for improved public health outcomes.
Addressing the workshop on the first day, Smt. Srivastava emphasised the need for a mission-mode approach to accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), supported by robust situational awareness and effective inter-departmental coordination. She highlighted the importance of leveraging digital health initiatives, particularly by strengthening linkages with the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) and Aarogya Setu, to facilitate integrated, coordinated and efficient healthcare delivery.
Addressing the participants on the second day, Smt. Srivastava highlighted the importance of strengthening the country's public health infrastructure, drawing upon the experiences and lessons of the COVID-19 pandemic. Recalling the need for rapid augmentation of healthcare facilities, research capabilities, genomic sequencing and vaccine development during the pandemic, she underlined that PM-ABHIM was conceived to enhance the country's preparedness to effectively respond to future pandemics and disease outbreaks.
She observed that while NHM contributes towards achieving key health-related Sustainable Development Goals through improved healthcare delivery, PM-ABHIM complements these efforts by strengthening the infrastructure, institutional capacities and systems required for public health resilience, emergency preparedness and pandemic response.
Smt. Srivastava highlighted that the Government, under the leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, has accorded emphasis to greater capital investment in the health sector and the promotion of public-private partnerships to strengthen healthcare infrastructure and service delivery.
Launched on 25 October 2021 with a financial outlay of ₹64,180 crore, PM-ABHIM aims to strengthen public health infrastructure, enhance disease surveillance and outbreak response capabilities, promote pandemic-related research and improve emergency preparedness and biosecurity. The Mission has approved 19,983 infrastructure units across the country, marking significant progress in the expansion of healthcare facilities, diagnostic capabilities and critical care infrastructure.
Under the Mission, grassroots healthcare infrastructure is being strengthened through the establishment of 11,001 Ayushman Arogya Mandir–Sub Health Centres at previously building-less locations and 5,456 Urban Ayushman Arogya Mandirs. The Free Drugs and Diagnostics Initiative further supports the availability of essential medicines and diagnostic services at these facilities, contributing to improved access to primary healthcare.
The diagnostic and disease surveillance network has also been strengthened through 2,151 Block Public Health Units and 744 district-level Integrated Public Health Laboratories. In addition, 631 Critical Care Blocks and 48 Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories have been supported under the Mission, enhancing capacities for timely diagnosis, disease management, critical care and research.
Highlighting the central sector interventions under PM-ABHIM, Smt. Srivastava referred to the establishment of branches of the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) in different parts of the country to strengthen disease surveillance, outbreak investigation and response. Other important interventions include the development of quarantine facilities at major airports, strengthening of points of entry at airports and ports, and the establishment of metropolitan surveillance units in 20 cities.
She also highlighted the Bharat Health Initiative for Sahyog Hita & Maitri (BHISHM) Cubes, which enable the rapid deployment of mini-hospital facilities during emergencies and are available through HLL for institutions requiring them. She further noted the support provided to the Department of Health Research for genomic sequencing research, which is important for strengthening the country's capacity to investigate and respond to emerging public health threats.
Emphasising the importance of robust disease surveillance systems, Smt. Srivastava highlighted the role of the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) and the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) in enabling timely identification and response to public health events. Information received through these platforms facilitates the Ministry's coordination and provision of support through the National Joint Outbreak Response Team.
IHIP is operational across all States and Union Territories, covering 50 health conditions and 12 national health programmes through more than 2.5 lakh public and private health facilities.
Smt. Srivastava underscored the importance of prioritisation, regular monitoring and close coordination between the Union Government and States and Union Territories to ensure the timely achievement of PM-ABHIM targets. She encouraged States and UTs to identify their infrastructure and capital investment requirements and share proposals that could be considered by the Union Government for further strengthening healthcare facilities across the country.
Calling for collective efforts towards effective implementation of the Mission, she urged States and UTs to work in close coordination with the Ministry to ensure that approved infrastructure is translated into functional facilities with the necessary equipment, human resources and operational arrangements. She emphasised that sustained Centre-State collaboration would be essential to strengthen the country's capacity to effectively respond to emerging public health challenges and future health emergencies.
The workshop featured technical sessions on the physical and financial progress of PM-ABHIM, along with presentations by States and Union Territories on implementation status, achievements and priorities. The discussions highlighted the importance of coordinated Centre-State efforts, regular monitoring and convergence of investments to ensure the timely operationalisation of infrastructure, improve healthcare service delivery and build a resilient public health system.
The workshop was attended by Shri Ritvik Ranjanam Pandey, Principal Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare, Government of Karnataka; Smt. Aradhana Patnaik, Additional Secretary and Mission Director, National Health Mission, Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Shri S. Akram Pasha, Mission Director, National Health Mission, Karnataka; senior officers and officials of the Ministry and representatives from States and Union Territories.

title: National Workshop on Unlocking Market-Based Financing under the Urban Challenge Fund
subtitle: There is need to change our approach towards urban development and build capacities in order to conceptualise and ground transformative projects across the urban landscape : Secretary, DoUD, MoHUA
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 NOV 2026 5:48PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Urban Development (DoUD), Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), organised a National Workshop on “Unlocking Market-Based Financing for Urban Challenge Fund Projects” on 26th November 2026 at Vanijya Bhawan, New Delhi. The workshop was held to help cities prepare bankable projects and move towards market-based financing of urban infrastructure.
Municipal Commissioners and Chiefs of Development Authorities from 25 million plus cities and State Mission Directors of the respective States took part in the workshop, along with sectoral experts and senior officials of DoUD, MoHUA. Financial institutions, including Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) and Housing and Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO), also participated. Knowledge institutions, including CEPT University, IIT Kharagpur, ISEG, Janaagraha, NIT Calicut, NIUA and SPA, supported the cities in the sessions.
The workshop provided handholding to cities on different aspects of preparing and financing urban projects. The sessions covered the UCF architecture, international examples of how projects under each vertical were financed, and reforms and enablers, including improving own-source revenue, the urban road reform initiative, city economic plans, carbon credit markets and the expectations of private investors. Also, session on PPPs covered project screening, structuring, risk allocation, revenue streams followed by city specific experiences.
Cities then worked in groups, each facilitated by a sectoral expert and knowledge institution, to ideate and structure priority projects for their cities based on learnings during the workshop and cross-learnings from other states, and reported their outcomes and proposed projects during the session.
The UCF has been designed as a shift from a grant-based approach to a market-linked, reform-driven and outcome-oriented framework for urban infrastructure. A Central Assistance of ₹1 lakh crore is provisioned to catalyse nearly ₹4 lakh crore of investment. Projects are bucketed under three verticals: Cities as Growth Hubs, Creative Redevelopment of Cities, and Water & Sanitation. So far, Projects worth more than ₹50,000 crore from 16 States/UTs have been approved through National Apex Committee meetings across all three verticals.
The projects are structured to attract private capital and market finance. Against the minimum requirement of 50 per cent mobilisation through loans, municipal bonds or PPPs, around 61 per cent has been proposed to be mobilised through these modes by the States. Pushing reforms in the cities is an integral part of the UCF and foundational to the challenge mode, with reforms ranging from digital, financial, planning and governance measures.
National Apex Committee meetings are held in the first week of every month under the chairmanship of Secretary, DoUD, MoHUA and some notable projects approved included Creative Redevelopment of Cities projects in Patna, Lucknow and Varanasi; Comprehensive development of Warangal city, Lucknow (waste-to-energy) and Tamil Nadu (smart metering, water treatment and waste-to-energy); and Cities as Growth Hubs projects in Assam (Sarusajai, Guwahati) and Sikkim (Gangtok Gateway).
Secretary DoUD, MoHUA emphasised, ‘There is need to change our approach towards urban development and build capacities in order to conceptualise and ground transformative projects across the urban landscape. The workshop is an affirmative step in that direction to equip cities with the skills and ideas required to submit bankable projects under UCF.’

title: Humane Character of the Story and Alignment with Gandhian Ideals Foremost Consideration for Evaluation: ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal Jury Member Manouj Kadaamh
content:
Goa, 26 November 2026
Ten fiction feature films are competing for the prestigious ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), exploring themes of peace, tolerance, empathy, social justice and intercultural dialogue. Member of the ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal jury
,
Shri Manouj Kadaamh and IFFI Creative Director Shri
Pankaj Saxena interacted with the media at a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) on the sidelines of the festival.
Speaking at the interaction, Shri Manouj Kadaamh highlighted the shared commitment of the selected films to using cinema as a medium to communicate meaningful ideas and promote a culture of peace.
Explaining the jury's approach to evaluating the films, Kadaamh said that the foremost consideration was the humane character of the story and its alignment with Gandhian ideals, particularly non-violence and the promotion of peace through cinema. A film's aesthetic and technical qualities, along with the sincerity and conviction with which the filmmaker communicates the intended message, were also important considerations, he said.
Referring to this year's IFFI theme, 'Stories Beyond Borders', he observed that the selected films had taken viewers across various parts of the world offering insights into unfamiliar cultures and perspectives. "Every film has its own potential and aesthetic values. It reflects the socio-economic and cultural aspects of that country. The films which are travelling the whole world are making the juries travel along with them to know their culture. That's the strength of cinema, which introduces you to the world," he said.
Highlighting some of the films in the competition, Kadaamh cited
Strawberries
as a portrayal of the struggle against injustice towards women and an affirmation of women's strength. He also pointed to
The Fall of the Queen
, which raises concerns about the patenting of medicines and access to healthcare, and
Scroll
, which carries an important message for the younger generation. He noted that several films go beyond depicting social problems and encourage audiences to think about workable solutions. He also opined that audience reactions alone could not alone determine a film's merit.
Speaking at the press conference, Pankaj Saxena,
Artistic Director of IFFI, said that the
ICFT-UNESCO mandate provided a clear framework for selecting films that promote tolerance, peace, understanding and intercultural exchange. He highlighted the responsibility of cinema in shaping society, cautioning that films could be both beneficial and harmful depending on how the medium is used.
Saxena noted that societies in the Global South, particularly those undergoing rapid social and cultural transitions, offer fertile ground for cinematic creativity. He added that films from countries such as Kenya, Haiti and Turkey provide audiences with valuable insights into evolving social realities and cultural dynamics.
He also emphasised that filmmakers need not always provide definitive solutions to social problems, as raising pertinent questions and stimulating public thought are equally essential functions of art. "An artist's job can be to provide solutions, but it can also be to leave open-ended questions. It is absolutely fine, and we care for artists of both types," he said.
Responding to a question on what enables stories to transcend geographical and cultural boundaries, Saxena identified aesthetics and relevance, or form and content, as the essential elements.
Shri Mahesh Kumar moderated the press conference.
About ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal
Instituted at the 46th edition of IFFI in collaboration with the International Council for Film, Television and Audiovisual Communication (ICFT), Paris, under the aegis of UNESCO, the ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal recognises films that reflect Mahatma Gandhi's ideals of non-violence, tolerance, intercultural understanding and a culture of peace. The ten films (seven International and three Indian) selected for this year's competition bring together stories from diverse cultural backgrounds, highlighting human relationships, social challenges and shared values.

title: Is Your Smartphone Controlling You? Tamil Thriller SCROLL Sparks a Digital Wake-Up Call at IFFI 2026

“A Thriller That Makes You Think, Not Preach”: Director Kannan S on Scroll and the Perils of Digital Addiction
content:
Goa, 26 November 2026
We scroll for a moment, stay for hours, chase the next notification and surrender to the next swipe. But what if the screen begins to scroll our lives instead? Exploring this unsettling possibility, Tamil feature film
Scroll
examines smartphone addiction, algorithmic manipulation and digital enslavement at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.
Director-producer Kannan S, along with lead actors Aravind Sundar and Kavya Anil, discussed the film's unconventional storytelling, experimental filmmaking techniques and contemporary themes at a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) on the sidelines of the festival.
Selected for the Indian Panorama section,
Scroll
is the only Tamil film nominated for the ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal at IFFI 2026. The 128-minute psychological thriller uses an innovative screen-life format, unfolding its narrative entirely through a mobile phone interface.
The film follows a young man battling smartphone addiction who downloads an application in an attempt to regain control of his life. What begins as a promise of digital liberation through gamified tasks and rewards soon turns into a cycle of disturbing challenges and psychological coercion.
Speaking about the film's nomination for the ICFT-UNESCO Gandhi Medal, director Kannan S highlighted the relevance of Gandhian values of truth, non-violence and self-restraint in an increasingly technology-driven world. Drawing inspiration from real-world digital phenomena such as the Blue Whale Challenge, he said the film seeks to encourage young audiences to reflect on unchecked digital dependence without sounding preachy. “We wanted to deliver a powerful social message through an engaging thriller rather than a lecture,” he remarked.
Kannan also spoke about the challenges of making a film entirely within a mobile phone interface. Most actors shot their portions independently from different locations, with several cast members meeting in person for the first time at the festival. “
The biggest challenge was to sustain cinematic tension within the limited frame of a mobile screen while keeping the narrative gripping and impactful
,” he explained.
Lead actor Aravind Sundar, who plays the protagonist, reflected on the irony of trying to overcome smartphone addiction through another application. He said everyday life itself became his preparation for the role, “
we are constantly rehearsing this reality every single day
.” He added that the film's distinctive format immerses audiences in the protagonist's claustrophobic digital world.
Kavya Anil highlighted the script's unconventional narrative and contemporary relevance. She said the film neither glorifies harmful digital challenges nor sensationalises their consequences but offers a thought-provoking examination of technology's ability to both connect and control.

title: “One Person’s Holiday, Another’s Home”: When Two Worlds Collide in A Few Days in the Sun at IFFI 2026
subtitle: A Thriller from Mexico’s Riviera Maya asks how Privilege and the Struggle to Survive can Bring People Closer than they Expect
content:
Goa, 26 November 2026
At a press conference held at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa today, director Mauro Mueller, writer José David Figueroa García and producer Leslie Holleran discussed their bilingual film A Few Days in the Sun, featured in the Cinema of the World section. The interaction offered insights into the film's making and creative vision.
In Mexico’s Riviera Maya, a wealthy European couple uses illegal ways to force a local community off the land planned for development. Meanwhile, a working-class Mexican family makes a risky deal with a corrupt police officer to keep a teenager out of prison. When their paths cross, both couples become involved in a violent kidnapping that quickly spirals out of control. Trapped in a harsh landscape, they must face the consequences of their actions and discover how privilege and the struggle to survive can bring them closer than they expected.
The film is an international co-production across five countries (Mexico, the Dominican Republic, Germany, the USA and Switzerland), in two languages (English and Spanish). At its core is a simple idea: one person’s holiday is another person’s home and daily life. What happens when these two worlds collide?
Mueller spoke about how much of his own life shaped the story and its perspective. He grew up in Switzerland and has also lived in Mexico and the USA. He believes that travelling and living in different countries is necessary to cultivate empathy, and to learn that there is no one way of living, and that no way of living is better or worse than another. Knowing languages and travelling, he added, helps us understand why people make different choices, and recognise how the systems and institutions around them shape the consequences of those same choices.
Mueller is no stranger to IFFI. His earlier film The Janitor (El Conserje) had its world premiere at the 56th IFFI in Goa in November 2025.
García emphasised the clash of cultures and social classes, a contrast that the film brings out clearly. He pointed out that when similar decisions are made, the wealthy European characters do not face the consequences that the working-class couple do, whose lives change drastically. Holleran echoed this, saying that for a poor person even the smallest mistake can bring everything crashing down. In the film, those holding the captives and the captives themselves are all, in a way, imprisoned by their circumstances.
García also explored how corruption runs through every level of society. At lower levels it is blunter, like bribery, while the wealthy couple’s attempt to illegally move a community off a piece of land is a higher-level corruption tied to power and politics, which is generally accepted. The film tries to place both kinds of corruption on the same level. Mueller and García also spoke about the widening inequality in the world, and how people are classified by their socio-economic class.
Mueller said the film aims to build empathy for why people make the morally grey choices they do. He chose the thriller genre to reach a newer and broader audience than a pure drama might. The result, he said, is a “character-driven thriller” standing at the border of arthouse and commercial cinema.
Holleran described the film as, in a way, women-focussed. The choices made by the women in both families, how they make them and how they connect to each other, drive much of the story. García added that stories of different classes clashing are relatable to everyone, as we all place ourselves in some class of society. By showing both sides facing similar dilemmas, the film invites viewers to understand, rather than ostracise, those from other classes, despite the difference in privilege.
Holleran said she finds inspiration when she sees something she recognises emotionally but is not a part of and wants to learn about it. The film’s exploration of outsiders entering a community comes from this. She also spoke about navigating the production process across so many producing countries. Discovering unfamiliar places `and collaborating with writers and directors, she said, is the best part of producing, along with meeting people from around the world. She spoke of falling in love with Mumbai, comparing its diversity and vibrance with her home city, New York.
Holleran observed that people worldwide are hungry for equality, recognition, and representation, and are trying to become comfortable with diversity as we find our way back to the arc of justice and fairness. She stressed the importance of travelling beyond the familiar, to hear a new language and to taste and smell a new culture. If people could travel more, she said, the world would be a better place.
Shri Labh Jain moderated the session.

title: “Stay Honest, Patient and True to Your Craft”: Mukesh Chhabra Shares the Secrets of Casting and Acting at IFFI 2026 Masterclass
subtitle:
“My Focus is to Bring an Oscar for this Country”: Mukesh Chhabra

No Age Barriers in Acting: Mukesh Chhabra Says Industry Needs Talent in their 40s, 50s and 60s
content:
Goa, 26 November 2026
Renowned casting director Mukesh Chhabra shared invaluable insights and practical tips for aspiring actors during a packed masterclass titled
The Casting Magic: Auditions Unplugged
, held today at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. The session witnessed an enthusiastic and diverse audience comprising aspiring actors, mid-career professionals looking to pursue acting, writers, emerging filmmakers and media representatives. Participants from across the country, along with a strong local Goan presence, actively engaged with Chhabra, raising a wide range of questions on what makes a good actor, how to ace an audition and the nuances of navigating the world of casting.
Speaking about Chhabra, Festival Director Ashutosh Gowariker said, “What I like about Mukesh is his eye for character and he will go to any length to find the actors who fit in.”
With over 300 films and web series to his credit, Chhabra offered a glimpse into the extensive and often painstaking process of casting, emphasising that discovering the right actor goes far beyond looking at databases or familiar faces. “There is so much talent in our country. Earlier, when there were no casting directors, it used to be difficult. I send my team everywhere to scout for talent. You have to go to the roots. Our country has so many cultural arts and sub-cultures where so much raw talent is displayed,” he said.
Explaining his approach to casting, Mukesh Chhabra said that he is often the first person a director approaches after a script is ready. He begins by reading the script thoroughly and discussing the characters and the director's vision. The next step involves deciding whether a role calls for an established actor or a fresh face, followed by travelling to the region where the story is set to discover talent among local communities. His job, he explained, is to understand the character, identify the right personality and recommend an actor who fits the director's vision. “Directors hire me for my opinion, my ideas, not for my data,” he observed, describing himself as a bridge between the actor and the director.
The scale of this process can be immense. Recalling the casting of Dangal, Chhabra revealed that it took nearly two years, with around 14,000 girls auditioning for the roles. The casting process for Ramayana, he said, extended over six years. He also recalled casting 384 people for Gangs of Wasseypur, a film that proved to be a major turning point in his career. “Gangs of Wasseypur changed my life", he informed.
Sharing his experience of working with noted filmmakers, Chhabra noted that every director has a distinct vision and approach. His responsibility is to ensure that the actors fit the characters as imagined by the filmmaker. Sometimes, he said, the casting process can even influence the writing. Citing
Kai Po Che!
, he recalled how the character of Gattu was written with Rajkummar Rao in mind. He also highlighted how talented actors such as Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Manoj Bajpayee bring their own strengths to a character, sometimes inspiring directors to rethink and reshape roles.
Reflecting on his journey of over two decades, Chhabra spoke about how actor Aamir Khan was among the first people to notice his work. He said that his journey has been driven by an enduring passion for discovering new talent. With around 100 more films lined up over the next two to three years, he remains deeply invested in the process.
The casting director's larger vision
Chhabra acknowledged that casting is an evolving creative exercise, with requirements changing from one film and script to another. Sometimes actors have to be replaced even at the last moment if someone else is found to be a better fit for the character. Such decisions, he explained, are part of the creative process and are guided by the needs of the film.
For Chhabra, casting is not merely a profession but a way of life. “Casting is not just a job for me. I do it for a living, this is life. My focus is to bring an Oscar for this country. I do my work honestly,” he said.
“Rejection is part of the journey”
Addressing one of the most pressing concerns among aspiring actors, Chhabra spoke candidly about rejection and the importance of resilience. “It's a part of your life, you've got to deal with this. We only have to find the right talent for a character. If you feel rejected and sad all the time, you will miss a lot of opportunities,” he said.
Drawing from his own experience, he revealed that his journey in the industry was far from easy. He began as an assistant director, initially working primarily on casting, and spent years establishing himself. Many directors had rejected him in his early days, he recalled, adding that some of those very filmmakers work with him today. “Every single person has to struggle in life. I don't want to talk about my sad story, but I really had a hard time,” he shared.
“Acting has nothing to do with age, talent is the only thing”
His advice to aspiring actors was to remain patient, positive and committed to their craft rather than becoming disheartened by the pace of their careers. “If you think you can act, do the job. Just go with it,” he said, adding that talent has no age barrier. “Acting has nothing to do with age, talent is the only thing.” He encouraged people in their 40s, 50s and 60s to pursue acting, pointing out that the industry needs performers across generations.
What makes an actor stand out?
For Chhabra, talent alone is not the only consideration when identifying the right actor for a role. Personality, honesty, simplicity and the ability to take directions are equally important. “The actor should also be directable. It's important to follow directions. Honesty and following instructions are important,” he said. “If you understand life and human emotions, you understand acting,” he added.
How to crack audition for a role?
Chhabra advises all aspiring actors going for audition to make sure that they understand the character and its background. “Designing the scene in your head is important. We want to understand the actor's intellect. Please do your homework”, he said.
On self-tapes, Chhabra recommended keeping the background clean and uncluttered, avoiding unnecessary make-up and ensuring that the performance remains the focus. The person reading the lines alongside the actor should provide appropriate cues, while the framing should include a close shot that captures the eyes and expressions clearly.
He also cautioned young actors against seeking constant validation on social media. Instead, they should focus on improving their craft, building confidence and gaining experience. Theatre, he said, is an excellent platform for developing confidence and honing acting skills. He particularly encouraged aspiring performers to join theatre groups and participate in stage productions, regardless of their age or previous experience.
He urged aspiring actors to maintain their purity and honesty, stay committed to learning and never allow impatience or the pursuit of instant recognition to derail their journey. “It is all a game of patience and positivity. If it is meant for you, it will come to you,” he said. “Be natural and simple”- is another mantra he gave to budding actors.
His masterclass offered a compelling reminder that behind every memorable on-screen character lies a painstaking process of discovery, preparation and collaboration. And for every aspiring actor, the journey begins with understanding people, respecting the craft and having the patience to wait for the right role.

title: What Makes a Life Meaningful? Kannada Documentary at 57th IFFI Seeks Answers in the Forest
subtitle: The Hug of Emptiness Explores Human Dignity, Resilience, and the Enduring Quest for Justice
content:
Goa, 26 November 2026
Kannada filmmaker Shri Pradeep Kumar Shetty K, also known as Dr. Pradeep Kenchanuru, addressed a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) in Goa today. He spoke about his documentary
The Hug of Emptiness
, featured in the Non-Feature Films section of Indian Panorama at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI). Made in 2025, the 20-minute film explores happiness, human dignity, and resilience through the life of a man who makes his home in a secluded forest after losing his property.
The film won the FIPRESCI International Critics Prize at the 19th Mumbai International Film Festival (MIFF) earlier this year.
The film follows Chandrashekhar, whose property, mortgaged to the Sullia Cooperative Bank in Karnataka, was taken over in 2003 after he was unable to repay a loan. Contesting the action, he embarked on a legal battle that has continued for over two decades. Meanwhile, he made a secluded stretch of forest his home, sustaining himself by weaving and selling baskets made from vines gathered there. His story brings together questions of justice, displacement, solitude, and human resilience.
Explaining what drew him to the subject, Shri Shetty said it was Chandrashekhar’s philosophy of life, rather than the legal dispute alone, that inspired the documentary. Despite living amid dense forests, heavy rainfall, and wildlife, without basic amenities such as electricity and roads, Chandrashekhar has found a rhythm and sense of purpose in everyday life. The director reflected that happiness could take different forms and need not always be defined by material comforts.
Speaking about his cinematic approach, Shri Shetty said he deliberately moved away from a conventional, interview-driven account of the legal dispute. Instead, the documentary observes the activities of a single day, allowing the rhythm of Chandrashekhar’s life and his relationship with the forest to unfold on screen.
On the film’s title, Shri Shetty said he drew philosophical inspiration from the works of Greek filmmaker Yorgos Lanthimos and their engagement with questions of human existence. For him, the title reflects the possibility of discovering meaning in a life that may appear empty to others.
A teacher by profession and a cinephile, Shri Shetty recalled his association with IFFI as a festival-goer since 2009. Speaking about the challenges of independent filmmaking, he revealed that the documentary was made on a budget of Rs. 4 lakhs, with financial support from a close friend who gave him creative freedom. title: Documentary of River Saraswati Explores the Mystery of an Ancient River Through the Lens of Science at IFFI 2026
subtitle: “Presenting an Extensive Body of Research in a Crisp, Engaging and Entertaining Format a Key Challenge”: Director Vishwanathan
content:
Goa, 26 November 2026
Hidden beneath the surface of the earth, flowing through the pages of ancient scriptures and embedded in India's civilisational memory, the Saraswati River has remained one of the country's enduring mysteries. Seeking to bridge the gap between ancient traditions and modern scientific inquiry, the Hindi documentary
The Unseen Holy River – Saraswati
, featured in the Indian Panorama category of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) 2026 today. The documentary explores the fascinating story of the river and the scientific investigations by Dr. Subash C. Singh surrounding the river’s existence. The film brings together ancient geographical references, geological observations and scientific investigations to present an intriguing exploration of India's natural and cultural heritage.
Addressing a Press Conference organised by PIB today, Director Bhasker Vishwanathan shared his experience of making his first documentary and said that the mystery surrounding the Saraswati River was equally fascinating for him, and that the research undertaken on the subject became a major source of inspiration. He highlighted the historical and cultural significance of the Saraswati, particularly its association with the Saraswat civilisation and the ancient Vedic tradition, with the Vedas believed to have been composed along its banks. Vishwanathan highlighted that presenting an extensive body of research in a crisp, engaging and entertaining format was a key challenge and his objective was to make the documentary appealing to a wider audience while retaining its research-oriented foundation.
Producer Abhinav M Jain shared that his motivation to produce the film stemmed from his curiosity about India's rivers and their historical significance. Recalling his visit to the Kumbh Mela at Prayagraj, he said that he observed only the Ganga and Yamuna at the Triveni Sangam which prompted him to explore the third river, Saraswati that finds repeated references in the Vedas and other Hindu scriptures. Highlighting the scientific dimension of the research, Jain referred to isotopic studies conducted by the National Institute of Hydrology, Roorkee, which examined water samples and contributed to the research surrounding the underground water network.
By bringing together geological research, ancient traditions and contemporary filmmaking, the documentary,
The Unseen Holy River – Saraswati,
offers audiences an opportunity to revisit a significant part of India's civilisational heritage through a scientific lens.
The press interaction was moderated by Shri. Swadhin Shakti Prasad.

title: Kyrgyz Drama ‘Skylark’ Brings Stories of Displacement, Memory and Resilience to IFFI
subtitle: Makers of the Grand Prix-winning film discuss Batken’s border realities, Kyrgyz folklore and childhood memories of Raj Kapoor and Mithun Chakraborty classics
content:
Goa, 26 November 2026
Director and screenwriter Narghiza Dotieva and producer Gulnara Kasmambetova addressed a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) in Goa today, following the India Premiere of their film
Skylark
in the International Competition section of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI). The filmmakers discussed the real-life experiences that inspired the film, its exploration of the human cost of post-Soviet border demarcations in Central Asia, and their longstanding affection for Indian cinema.
The 85-minute Kyrgyz drama draws on real events and news reports from the Kyrgyzstan-Tajikistan border, where newly drawn boundaries have separated communities that lived together for centuries. The film follows teenager Aibek, who is raised by his grandmother Ene. After her passing, Aibek faces a poignant moral and emotional test as he strives to fulfil her final wish, to be buried beside her husband in a cemetery that now lies across the border in Tajikistan.
Winner of the Grand Prix at the Amur Autumn Film Festival 2026,
Skylark
blends Central Asian oral storytelling with contemporary cinema.
Dotieva explained that the film draws inspiration directly from events along the border, while Kasmambetova highlighted how sudden divisions transformed familiar pastures and ancestral burial grounds in the Batken region into restricted zones. In Kyrgyz folklore, the skylark nesting peacefully on the back of a sheep symbolises peace and harmony, anchoring the film’s message of human endurance amid conflict.
Reflecting on their cultural bond with India, the filmmakers recalled how Indian cinema shaped their childhoods in Soviet-era Kyrgyzstan. They remembered watching Bollywood films with their families and gathering with neighbourhood children in courtyards to sing songs and imitate Mithun Chakraborty’s dance moves from
Disco Dancer
. Indian films, they said, offered a vital “fresh window of emotions” in a society where public expressions of romance were subdued.
The director also noted that Indian cinema, from Raj Kapoor’s classics to films starring Amitabh Bachchan, resonated across generations in Kyrgyzstan for its warmth, storytelling and celebration of human connection. The session was moderated by Brinda Randeep Sudan.

title: IFFI Campus Offers an Experience Beyond Cinema, Celebrating India’s Creative and Cultural Diversity
subtitle: Festival Reaffirms Commitment to an Inclusive Experience for All in Collaboration with Svayam
content:
Goa, 26 November 2026
At the ongoing 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Panaji, the festival experience extends well beyond the silver screen. The IFFI campus has evolved into a vibrant meeting ground for creative institutions, cultural initiatives, regional cuisines, local products, merchandise and accessibility initiatives. Together, these diverse offerings provide delegates, filmmakers, students and visitors with an opportunity to discover and engage with India’s rich creative and cultural landscape.
Advancing Accessibility and Inclusion
An important feature of the campus is the awareness initiative by Svayam, an organisation working towards dignity and accessibility for persons with reduced mobility. Participating at IFFI for the second time, Svayam is drawing attention to the need for accessible public spaces and the participation of persons with disabilities in cultural and social activities. The initiative complements accessibility arrangements across the festival venue, reinforcing the importance of making cultural experiences accessible and welcoming to all.
Showcasing India's Creative and Educational Ecosystem
The festival campus also serves as a platform for institutions working across creative technology, cinema, performing arts and design to present their initiatives and interact with visitors.
The Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT), Mumbai, India’s National Centre of Excellence for Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics and Extended Reality (AVGC-XR), is also engaging visitors through an animation character-making competition. Its merchandise display further introduces visitors to the possibilities and growing opportunities within the creative technology sector.
The Directorate of Publications Division (DPD) is presenting a collection of publications on Indian cinema, alongside its iconic Gandhian series. Special discounts on select titles are adding to the appeal, encouraging visitors to explore its literary offerings.
The participation of the SA Film Academy, Chennai; Dada Lakshmi Chand State University of Performing and Visual Arts, Rohtak, Haryana; and JD Institute of Fashion Technology further reflects the breadth of academic and professional disciplines contributing to India's expanding media, entertainment and creative industries.
A taste of regional diversity
Food stalls add another dimension to the campus experience, bringing together a variety of regional and popular choices. ranging from traditional Naga cuisine and biryani to dosa, coffee and bakery products. Adding a distinct Goan touch, the Goa Forest Development Corporation Limited is showcasing locally sourced cashew nuts, highlighting the region's indigenous produce.
Merchandise outlets offer visitors a range of festival memorabilia and creative products. The Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), Pune, is displaying clothing and accessories, while the Entertainment Society of Goa (ESG) is also presenting its own collection of merchandise.
Entertainment beyond the Big Screen
Extending the festival experience into the digital and broadcast space, Prime Video, Story TV App and BIG FM are also participating through their respective stalls. Their presence offers visitors an opportunity to engage with diverse formats and platforms across the evolving media and entertainment landscape.
Stall operators appreciated the support extended by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Entertainment Society of Goa and the National Film Development Corporation in facilitating their participation.
With its mix of creative institutions, regional flavours, local products, entertainment platforms and accessibility initiatives, the IFFI campus offers visitors a space to discover, interact and engage with the many facets of India's cultural and creative landscape.

title: Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti Organises the Second Regional Conference at Agra
subtitle:
​​​​​​​Union Jal Shakti Minister Shri C.R. Paatil said that access to tap connections must be complemented by assured delivery of safe drinking water to rural households

Seven Northern States and Union Territories deliberate on accelerating implementation and ensuring long-term functionality of rural drinking water supply schemes
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 NOV 2026 7:17PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India, organised the Second Regional Conference on Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) 2.0 at Agra, Uttar Pradesh, bringing together representatives of seven northern States and Union Territories to deliberate on key strategies for accelerating implementation, strengthening sustainability and ensuring long-term functionality of rural drinking water supply systems. The conference forms part of a series of regional consultations being organised following the Departmental Summit on Water and provides a platform for States and Union Territories to review progress, share best practices and discuss solutions to common challenges.
Senior officials from Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh participated in the conference along with representatives from the National Jal Jeevan Mission, State Water and Sanitation Missions, line Ministries
viz.
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MoSDE), and Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD). Deliberations focused on sustainability, institutional reforms, convergence, operation and maintenance, groundwater management and community-led water governance.
During the ministerial session, a
Jal Kalash ceremony
was performed by the dignitaries, symbolising respect for water and reaffirming the collective resolve towards water conservation, source sustainability and responsible water management.
Chairing the Ministerial Session at the Conference,
Union Minister of Jal Shakti Shri C.R. Paatil
highlighted the transformative impact of Jal Jeevan Mission in improving the quality of life in rural India and reducing the drudgery faced by women and girls. Referring to the vision of Hon'ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi for ensuring water security, he emphasised that while significant progress has been made in providing tap water connections across rural households, the next phase of Jal Jeevan Mission must focus on ensuring regular, adequate and safe drinking water supply through sustainable and community-owned service delivery systems.
Further, the Union Minister added that sustainability should remain at the core of all efforts under JJM 2.0. He also underlined the need for timely implementation, greater accountability and collaborative action by States and Union Territories to achieve the Mission's objectives.
Referring to
Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari se Jan Aandolan
, Shri Paatil highlighted the importance of transforming water conservation into a people's movement through active community participation. He emphasised the need to promote groundwater recharge, rainwater harvesting and source protection measures through convergence with ongoing development programmes. Stressing that water conservation is a shared responsibility, he called upon States to strengthen community ownership through initiatives such as Jal Arpan and Jal Utsav and to actively exchange best practices for ensuring sustainable drinking water services for every rural household.
Shri S. P Singh Baghel, Union Minister (Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairyings; Panchayati Raj) and Member of Parliament from Agra,
highlighted the importance of sustained coordination among the Central and State Governments, district administrations and implementing agencies in addressing drinking water challenges and ensuring water security. Referring to the regional context, he noted the significance of effective water resource management and inter-regional coordination in ensuring adequate water availability. He expressed confidence that the deliberations during the conference would contribute to identifying practical solutions for strengthening reliable and sustainable rural drinking water services.
Welcoming the delegates,
Shri Swatantra Dev Singh, Cabinet Minister for Jal Shakti and Flood Control, Uttar Pradesh,
highlighted the remarkable progress achieved under Jal Jeevan Mission in the State. He noted that tap water coverage in rural Uttar Pradesh has expanded significantly since 2019, with drinking water supply schemes being implemented across the State through a transparent and accelerated approach despite operational  challenges. He said that sustained efforts have led to substantial improvement in rural drinking water access, with work on the remaining schemes progressing rapidly towards universal coverage.
Referring to the water-stressed regions of Bundelkhand and Vindhya, Shri Singh highlighted the transformative impact of Jal Jeevan Mission in addressing long-standing drinking water challenges. He noted that districts which once faced acute water scarcity and seasonal distress have witnessed significant improvements in access to safe drinking water through household tap connections. Emphasising the importance of knowledge sharing and collaborative learning, he observed that the Regional Conference provides an important platform for States and Union Territories to exchange experiences, share best practices and strengthen implementation strategies for ensuring sustainable rural drinking water service delivery.
Secretary, DDWS, Shri Ashok K.K Meena
, highlighted that sustainability of rural drinking water services requires a whole-of-government approach and cannot be achieved through the drinking water sector alone. He emphasised the importance of convergence across sectors, including skilling, source sustainability, financing, Panchayati Raj institutions and community ownership, for ensuring long-term functionality of rural water supply systems.
Emphasising the need to move beyond infrastructure creation, Shri Meena called upon States and Union Territories to focus on source sustainability, sustainable operation and maintenance, financial planning, skilled local manpower and strengthened Gram Panchayat-led governance. He highlighted the role of tools such as the Decision Support System (DSS) for evidence-based planning, end-to-end digital mapping of water supply assets under Sujalam Bharat Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) and empowerment of Gram Panchayats, Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs) for improving service delivery, accountability and long-term sustainability.
During another session
of the conference
Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, AS&MD, NJJM,
outlined the need for transitioning from infrastructure development to sustainable rural drinking water service delivery under Jal Jeevan Mission 2. It was highlighted that the focus would be on ensuring regular, adequate and quality drinking water supply through effective operation and maintenance of existing infrastructure for the next 25–30 years. The importance of clearly defined roles and responsibilities of district administrations, District Magistrates and Panchayati Raj Institutions at all levels was underscored for ensuring long-term sustainability of rural water supply systems.
Shri Soan also shared about the importance of inter-departmental convergence among Public Health Engineering, Rural Development, Panchayati Raj, Skill Development and Tribal Affairs Departments for strengthening source sustainability and O&M. It was informed that five regional conferences were being organised to deliberate on key reforms and implementation strategies, with their outcomes to be reviewed at a national-level conference. The consolidated progress would subsequently be presented to the Hon’ble Prime Minister, with collective efforts of the Centre, States and local institutions being emphasised for achieving the objectives of Jal Jeevan Mission by December 2028.
Shri D. Senthil Pandiyan, Joint Secretary, DDWS,
during the presentation by representatives of MoRD, emphasised the importance of source sustainability through geotagging of drinking water sources and implementation of the Decision Support System (DSS). Highlighting the integration of data from six departments and agencies to identify at-risk water sources, he urged States to undertake physical verification, pre- and post-monsoon water quality testing, and prepare village-level source augmentation plans through convergence with Rural Development and Panchayati Raj institutions and integration with GPDP. States were requested to expedite geotagging, water quality testing and DSS implementation, and update progress by 31 December 2026.
As the conference coincided with
Constitution Day
, the dignitaries and participants also jointly read the
Preamble to the Constitution of India
, reiterating their commitment to the constitutional values of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
The key reform pillars under Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 were presented by
Shri Y.K. Singh, Director, NJJM
with emphasis on strengthening Gram Panchayats and district-level institutions for sustainable rural water service delivery. The importance of performance benchmarking, healthy competition, third-party inspections, water quality monitoring, source sustainability and digital governance through the Sujalam Bharat portal was highlighted. States were urged to expedite the creation of Sujalam Bharat IDs, GIS-based asset tagging and pipeline mapping, and strengthen community participation through Har Ghar Jal certification, Jal Arpan, Jal Seva Arpan and Jal Utsav initiatives.
The need for time-bound capacity building of Gram Panchayat functionaries, VWSC members and district technical teams was underscored, along with the deployment of trained Nal Jal Mitras to strengthen village-level operation and maintenance. States were also encouraged to formulate O&M policies, adopt preventive maintenance practices, ensure financial sustainability, and promote research, innovation and outcome-based financing. The importance of adhering to the timelines for implementing the identified reforms, which were linked to the payment mechanism, was emphasised to ensure smooth financial flows and sustainable drinking water service delivery
.
Shri Y.K. Singh further presented on
Institutional and Financial Sustainability
, highlighting the utilisation of 16th Finance Commission tied grants earmarked for water and sanitation to strengthen the financial capacity of Gram Panchayats for operation and maintenance of rural water supply systems. The importance of integrating these resources with other convergence funds and user-charge collections and incorporating water and sanitation activities into GPDPs, was emphasised. Priority areas such as source sustainability, water quality management, electricity costs, solarisation of water supply schemes, drainage and greywater management were also highlighted to ensure sustainable service delivery at the village level.
Smt. Kritika Kulhari, Deputy Secretary, NJJM,
presented on PMJANMAN and DAJGUA and highlighted the progress and implementation requirements, emphasising the need to ensure saturation of rural drinking water supply in identified tribal habitations. She focused on the need to ensure drinking water coverage in all identified PVTG and tribal-majority habitations within the stipulated timelines.
States were requested to submit complete proposals in accordance with the prescribed DPR checklist, supported by Chief Secretary-led Apex Committee approval, joint certification by the Tribal Affairs and concerned water supply departments, non-duplication certificates and appropriate technical justifications. States were urged to coordinate with their respective Tribal Affairs Departments to identify any uncovered habitations, update records and submit complete proposals at the earliest to facilitate timely approval and implementation of drinking water supply schemes.
Representatives from the
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MoSDE), Shri Avinash Kishore
presented on the skilling of Nal Jal Mitras, Sujalam Shakti and skill formalization and highlighted ongoing efforts to strengthen skill ecosystems and capacity-building initiatives for rural water sector personnel, including local technicians, Plumbers, Masonry, Electricians and operators.
Shri Gowri Shankar and Shri Raj Kishore Singh
, officials from
Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD),
delivered a detail presentation highlighting convergence opportunities with programmes such as VB-G RAM G for creation of water conservation structures, source strengthening measures, support for sustainability interventions and incorporation of Sujalam Shakti.
Senior officials from the participating States and Union Territories made presentations focusing on updates on progress achieved under the Mission and shared experiences related to state initiatives, digital interventions, IEC, convergence, implementation of sustainability measures, institutional reforms and community participation initiatives.
Delegates exchanged best practices and discussed emerging challenges related to source sustainability, functionality of schemes, operation and maintenance, capacity building and financial sustainability. Participants also deliberated on innovative approaches adopted at the State level for improving service delivery and strengthening governance systems.
The conference featured deliberations on implementation of Comprehensive Implementation and Reform Plans (CIRPs), sustainable operation and maintenance, source sustainability, financial sustainability and institutional strengthening. Participants also discussed community ownership, Panchayat-led water governance, capacity development and inter-ministerial convergence as key enablers for ensuring long-term functionality and sustainable rural drinking water service delivery under JJM 2.0.
The second day of the conference will undertake field visits to five selected rural drinking water supply schemes and villages in Uttar Pradesh to observe Jal Arpan and best practices in service delivery, source sustainability, operation and maintenance and community-led water governance. The field exposure is expected to facilitate cross-learning and support replication of successful models across participating States and Union Territories.

title: Updated edition of the Constitution of India released in all 22 Scheduled Languages on Constitution Day 2026
subtitle:
Vice President of India Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan graces the occasion at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi

Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Law and Justice Shri Arjun Ram Meghwal also addresses the gathering
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                26 NOV 2026 4:31PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Legislative Department of the Ministry of Law and Justice, celebrated Constitution Day 2026 with a special programme at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi, marking the release of the updated edition of the Constitution of India in all 22 Scheduled Languages. The programme was graced by the Vice President of India, Shri C. P. Radhakrishnan, as the Chief Guest, in the presence of Shri Arjun Ram Meghwal, Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Law and Justice, and Dr. Rajiv Mani, Secretary, Legislative Department and Department of Legal Affairs.
The programme commenced with the National Song and National Anthem, followed by the ceremonial lighting of the lamp by the Vice President and the Minister. A short film highlighting the initiative was screened. The film described the Constitution not merely as a publication but as an enduring symbol of the struggle, dedication, cultural heritage, linguistic pride and democratic consciousness of the people of India, and as the charter that guarantees every citizen equality, liberty, justice and fraternity. It recalled the inclusive, equal and just India envisioned by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar and the members of the Constituent Assembly, and the vital role of Indian languages in realising that vision. It also emphasised that the initiative would bring the Constitution closer to citizens in rural areas, tribal communities and the younger generation, and concluded with the resolve that the Constitution should not remain confined to Parliament and the courts but should reach every village, every home, every school and every citizen.
The Vice President then released the updated edition of the Constitution of India in all 22 Scheduled Languages. This marks an important step towards promoting constitutional awareness and making the country’s supreme law accessible to citizens across linguistic backgrounds.
In his special address, the Vice President underscored the enduring significance of the Constitution and its role in upholding the values of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. He also emphasised the importance of making constitutional knowledge accessible to every citizen.
Addressing the gathering, Union Minister Shri Arjun Ram Meghwal recalled the contribution of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, Member of the Constituent Assembly and Chairman of the Drafting Committee, in giving the nation a forward-looking Constitution that rests on the pillars of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. He described the Constitution as the foundation of India’s democratic framework and stressed the need to strengthen citizens’ awareness of their constitutional rights and duties.
Dr. Rajiv Mani delivered the welcome address and highlighted the significance of Constitution Day and the Department’s efforts to make the Constitution and other laws accessible to citizens in their own languages. He thanked all those who contributed to making this momentous occasion possible, noting that this is the first time since the Constitution came into force that an updated edition of the Constitution is available in all 22 Scheduled Languages.
The release of the updated edition of the Constitution of India in all 22 Scheduled Languages reflects the Government’s commitment to promoting inclusive access to constitutional knowledge, strengthening constitutional literacy and bringing the ideals of the Constitution closer to every citizen.
